newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - British magazine offers help to homeless.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - British magazine offers help to homeless.

text.p: "Big Issue," cries Alex from a makeshift pavement pitch as he tries to hawk his pile of magazines to shoppers hurrying into a London supermarket.
Alex and thousands of other Big Issue vendors have become a part of Britain's urban landscape since the colourful weekly was set up in 1991 to help the growing army of homeless people.

The vendors, drawn largely from the ranks of the homeless, pay 35 pence (57 cents) for the magazine but sell it for 80p. The difference provides them with a lifeline as they struggle to pull themselves out of the poverty trap.
"I used to beg but I make more money this way," says Alex, a burly, bearded figure, wrapped up against the cold in a heavy lumberjack coat and woollen hat.
"I sell about 40 copies a day. A lot of people give me a quid (pound) so I make about 20 quid," added the 43-year-old Scotsman, saying the money enabled him to live in a squat.
Big Issue publisher Andrew Jaspan, former editor of the prestigious Observer Sunday newspaper, said the magazine really can improve the grim lot of Britain's underclass.
"It has changed the lives of people who were down and out," said Jaspan. "Once they are allocated a pitch they have to get their finances together and get used to time-keeping."
MAGAZINE HAS SPAWNED IMITATORS AROUND GLOBE
The vendors, who number in excess of 3,000 nationally, are given two weeks' training before they are issued with their identity badge and a starter-pack of 10 free copies.
Jaspan said that vendors start to save money and move out of street doorways and into hostels before some find permanent accommodation.

The magazine does not cut off vendors as soon as they have a place to live. Instead it tries to provide training and put them in touch with potential employers as they move back towards mainstream society.
It has spawned imitators around the globe. Australian and South African Big Issues have been launched and there are plans to take the idea to New York at some point.

The Big Issue found itself at the centre of Britain's pre-election political debate at the turn of the year when Tony Blair, leader of the opposition Labour Party, gave an interview to the magazine in which he backed a crackdown on petty crime, so-called "zero tolerance" policing.

Blair added that he wanted to see homelessness, which grew alarmingly in the 1980s as welfare benefits were cut, tackled at its roots to end the need for begging and for people to sleep on the streets.
Jaspan said the Blair interview and huge attendant publicity helped to boost the credibility of a magazine which now sells some 270,000 copies weekly across Britain.
The Big Issue plans interviews with Conservative Prime Minister John Major and Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown in the run-up to the election, which must be held by May.
CRITICS SAY PEOPLE BUY BIG ISSUE TO EASE CONSCIENCES

Printed on low-grade paper, the magazine mixes reports on social issues with rock and film reviews and is especially popular among the young. It produces northern, Scottish and Welsh editions to complement its core London issue.
Its 60-strong London editorial and production team come from the world of professional journalism. However, critics maintain that people buy the magazine only to ease their consciences.
"We are halfway along the road between being a "pity purchase' and being bought for our content," said Jaspan.
"But the week when we had the George Michael interview we added 120,000 sales -- they weren't all people who were feeling extra charitable."
The magazine pulled off a coup last year when it ran a candid interview with introspective pop star Michael, who had not spoken to the press for several years.
The Big Issue makes a profit but ploughs all its earnings into a foundation which provides support services such as training, housing advice and drug and alcohol counselling.
Homeless charity Shelter says that the Big Issue plays a role in helping those who are still able to help themselves but must not be seen as a panacea for the problems of the homeless.
"The worry is that governments may become complacent and leave it to the Big Issue," said Shelter's Susan Littlemore.
"The very young, 16 and 17-year-olds, and those who have been on the street for some time still need help."
Official figures for 1995 listed 360,000 homeless but Shelter says that tally is "the tip of the iceberg", as it excludes many youngsters who have never registered for state benefits.
Alex, who has spent a lifetime sleeping rough or in hostels, agrees the magazine has been a boost for him. But he is downbeat about his chances of moving back to conventional employment.
"I gave up selling and tried to get a job but employers said I was too old," he said. "People reckon it'll be easier if Labour win the election but I don't think so." ($1=.6119 Pound)
